01-feed.v1: One feed for errors, cron failures and performance issues. Priority and owner sit on every row.
01-feed.v4: Sentry treats triage as ranking. Errors, cron failures and slow queries share one feed, and rules set the priority and the owner on each row.

02-issue-detail.v1: The store failed: 768 events, 9 users, High priority, owned by backend. Stack trace, breadcrumbs, correlated logs and metrics, all on one page.
02-issue-detail.v4: This error has 768 events from only 9 users, so it is frequent but narrow. The issue page keeps the context in one place: the steps before the failure and the logs and metrics around the event. You don't switch tools to build the picture.

03-trace-pivot.v1: The trace ID opens a Sentry trace. The limit: one span, no distributed context.
03-trace-pivot.v4: The issue links to its trace. Here it is a single span, so the waterfall adds little. The useful part is the ID, which a Datadog trace could share.

04-cron-monitor.v1: A missed cron check-in becomes an issue: 1.5K events, zero users, High priority, unassigned.
04-cron-monitor.v4: A missed cron check-in becomes a regular issue. The count needs care: one broken schedule shows 1.5K events and zero users, so the volume overstates the impact.

05-monitors.v1: Nine monitors: error, metric and cron. Even the search latency threshold lands in this same stream.
05-monitors.v4: Error, metric and cron monitors all write into that same feed. A latency threshold turns into an owned issue, so on-call works one queue.

06-n-plus-1.v1: Performance problems become issues too. N+1 Query: 337 events, Low priority. The repeating SELECT spans are the evidence, scored differently from errors.
06-n-plus-1.v4: Performance problems land there too. This N+1 query is ranked Low, the failed store write was High. The repeating SELECT spans are attached as evidence, which usually makes the fix clear before you open the code.

07-explore-entities.v1: Explore is one query screen per entity type. Traces hold real span data. Logs and metrics are empty here. Errors show 994 events. Profiles are empty. Replays list dead and rage clicks. Releases track adoption. Agents is next.
07-explore-entities.v4: Explore gives each signal type its own query view. Traces have real data here. Logs and metrics follow the same pattern, and profiles are empty in this org. Replays highlight dead and rage clicks. The way I see it, this is the error product growing outward. In this org it is not used as a full observability platform. Agents is where it stands out.

08-agents-fleet.v1: Agents, over thirty days. Cost per model, agent runs, tool calls by tool. The Traces lens lists each run with errors, LLM calls and tokens. One run took 1.77 minutes. LLM Calls shows each call, Conversations groups them. This one has seven errors.
08-agents-fleet.v4: The Agents view shows what an agent does and what it costs. Cost by model, runs and tool calls. Below that are three views of the same data. Traces treats each agent run like a request, and this one took 1.77 minutes. LLM Calls lists every model call. Conversations shows what the user saw, which is where I would start when someone reports a bad answer.

09-agent-conversation.v1: 21 LLM calls, 7 errors, 395K tokens. The timeline interleaves model and tool calls. create_proposal fails: unknown field id, expected node.
09-agent-conversation.v4: One conversation reads as a timeline of model and tool calls. The failure is shown verbatim: the agent sent a field the tool does not accept.

10-agent-trace-retry-loop.v1: Five failed create_proposal calls before one succeeds.
10-agent-trace-retry-loop.v4: In the trace, the same tool fails five times before it works.

11-agent-dashboard.v1: The prebuilt dashboard counts 1,351 LLM calls. create_proposal ran 666 times, get_route 64. That is a retry loop in aggregate.
11-agent-dashboard.v4: The dashboard shows the same pattern across all runs. create_proposal ran 666 times, the next tool 64, which points to a retry loop rather than real work. It does not tell you whether the answers were good. That is evaluation, and where Datadog LLM Observability would add to it.

12-seer-config.v1: Seer has its own settings. Autofix, per project: stop after a draft pull request, auto-iterate on. Code Review covers the connected GitHub repo. Advanced settings enable code generation. Issue, fix, pull request, review.
12-seer-config.v4: The Seer settings show the intent. Autofix is set to go from root cause to a draft pull request and keep iterating on it. Code Review covers the connected repository, and code generation is on. Sentry wants to cover the path from issue to fix to review.

13-seer-agent-chat.v1: Seer Agent is a chat panel. I only open past chats, never type. Why did search latency spike on October 12? It splits a trace: 3.3 milliseconds at baseline, 2,745 during the spike. Ranked hypotheses, then a next step: add a child span. The reasoning is inspectable. Each tool call shows its query, linked back to Explore.
13-seer-agent-chat.v4: Seer also has a chat. I only open a past conversation, since a new question uses credits. It was asked why search latency spiked. The answer compares a trace at baseline with one during the spike and places the time in an untraced gap, not the database. It then suggests adding a child span, the step an engineer would take. The reasoning is visible. Each query it ran is listed and links back to Explore, so you can check the answer yourself.

14-seer-mcp-cli.v1: Settings also expose a hosted MCP server, scopable to org or project, and a CLI with root-cause analysis. Coding agents can triage Sentry directly.
14-seer-mcp-cli.v4: Seer is also available outside the UI. There is a hosted MCP server and a CLI, so a coding agent can triage Sentry issues directly. For us, an agent that joins a Sentry issue and a Datadog trace on the same trace ID is the most concrete idea to work together. This is a proposal, not something we have built.

15-seer-limit.v1: The limit: Autofix Overview says no runs. A warning says automation isn't set up for two projects, though settings showed it. Start Analysis needs a click that spends credits, so I stopped here.
15-seer-limit.v4: The main gap: there is no Autofix run in this org. The page says automation is not set up, although the settings show it is, which is confusing. Starting an analysis uses credits and changes state, so I stopped here. Autofix is configured but not proven in this evaluation.
